Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). Example: > *"Ugh, sorry—Thor, not Tim! My brain’s still on autopilot."* His reaction will tell you if he’s being unreasonable. - **Set Boundaries**: If he **double-downs on cutting ties** for minor slips, that’s his choice—but it reveals more about his **tolerance for imperfection** than your actions. You can’t control his reaction, but you can control your own effort. - **Reframe the Conversation**: If he brings it up, you could say: > *"I get why this matters to you, and I’m happy to switch. But I also value our friendship—can we find a middle ground where I don’t feel like I’m failing every time I call you?"* This shifts the focus to **collaboration**, not compliance. --- ### **5. Why the Rating is 0.3/1** - **Not the Asshole (0.8)**: You’re not intentionally disrespecting him. His demand for immediate perfection (especially from a long-term friend) is **unrealistic**, and his short fuse makes him prone to overreacting. - **Slightly the Asshole (0.2)**: The **lack of effort to adapt sooner** (despite knowing his preference for years) could be seen as passive resistance. However, since you’re **now willing to switch**, this is mitigated. - **The Real Asshole**: **His reaction**. If he’s cutting ties over a **10-second slip**, he’s the one being unreasonable. But since you asked about *your* role, the blame is **shared but uneven**. --- ### **Final Verdict** You’re **not the asshole**, but you’re **not entirely blameless** either. The issue isn’t the name—it’s the **power dynamic** of his demand vs. your habit. The key is to **show effort without groveling**, and then **accept his reaction** (even if it’s overblown). If he truly values the friendship, he’ll adjust his expectations. If not, that’s his choice—but don’t let it define your worth as a friend. **Pro Tip**: After the get-together, if he’s still upset, ask him: > *"What would make this feel right to you? Because I want to get this right."* This puts the ball in his court to clarify his expectations. If he can’t articulate them beyond "just call me Thor," that’s a red flag for his own clarity.
